correctness.rationale: For all odd primes p, e>=2 and primitive roots b modulo p^e, the inverse-parity equivalence is reconstructed by explicit nonnegative solutions for each parity and excludes the opposite equation. Summing the even unit residues gives S=(p-1)(p^(2e-1)+1)/4 and 4S congruent p-1 modulo p^e, so S is a unit. Any output period t stabilizes the even-unit set under multiplication by b^(-t); summing then implies b^t=1, forcing phi(p^e)|t. The modular state word supplies the reverse divisibility. The unique involution -1 flips parity at half period. A separate standard-library verifier checked 33 moduli, 272 primitive bases, 75882 positions, 355 direct equation predicates, and nonprimitive behavior. No finite check is used as the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The directly read arXiv:2609.08728v1 establishes only a period dividing the multiplicative order. Older d-sequences cover the prime-modulus phenomenon, and OEIS A167791 plus binary reciprocal digit interpretation cover some prime powers with primitive base 2; neither provides the asserted all-generator theorem on arbitrary odd prime powers, notably moduli such as 49 where 2 has order 21 but base 3 has order 42. The exact uniform full-period result is not implied by the source upper bound nor the listed special cases. Explicit checks of related wording, prime-power lift, OEIS tables and indexed published findings found no known covering theorem. Literature search cannot demonstrate absolute novelty, and one plausible period paper was only abstract-accessible.
residual_risks: The full Thippireddy-Chalasani 2008 recursive-generator period paper was not obtained; it may include a relevant general lemma.
A result under an unindexed or different generator terminology may cover all primitive bases; searches cannot rule that out.
Related base-2 and prime-modulus results are explicitly known, so the novelty claim is only for the uniform all-primitive-generator odd prime-power class.

value.rationale: The 2026 motivating work studies exactly this Diophantine solvability word and leaves its least period undetermined beyond an upper bound. Determining whether a natural two-valued observation loses the full primitive-root state period is a substantive exact invariant. The theorem closes this classification for every odd prime-power modulus and every primitive root, including composite moduli with nonprimitive base 2 (e.g. 49,3). The sum of even reduced residues provides a structural trivial-stabilizer lemma, with consequences of exact half-period complement and balance. An explicit nonprimitive counterexample displays why equality is not automatic. No downstream paper-sized theorem is presumed.
